Issued at 308 AM CDT Thu Oct 15 2026

Though Tonight:

Per recent GOES-19 water vapor imagery, an upper-level trough 
is lifting northeastward across the Rocky Mountains toward the 
central Plains ahead of a vigorous northern-stream trough 
digging southeastward into the Dakotas. Pressure falls on the 
order of 1 to 2 mb/hr have commenced in central Oklahoma (likely
augmented by convection), which will spread northeastward with 
time as the lead upper-level trough lifts atop a southwest- to 
northeastward-oriented low-level baroclinic zone stretching 
into the Great Lakes. Generally speaking, the forecast for the 
next 24 to 48 hours remains on track with the expectation for
the first fall storm of the season to move through the Great
Lakes region. As this occurs, a myriad of weather conditions 
will occur in our local area. 

After daybreak, showers and areas of drizzle (already developing
at press time) will gradually expand across northern Illinois 
and northwestern Indiana. As our area will be somewhat removed 
from the strongest forcing (warm conveyer belt focused just 
south of our area, and increasing frontogenetical forcing 
focused to our north), am not expecting hefty precipitation 
totals through the first half of the day. Coverage of showers 
and drizzle should maximize this afternoon as the surface low 
moves directly over our area, though again coverage may be more 
scattered than widespread owing to somewhat disjointed forcing.
Nevertheless, seasonably high PWATs (nearing 2 inches) will 
support torrential downpours where showers are most persistent 
this afternoon. 

Am seeing quite a bit of variance in the exact track of the 
surface low in high-res guidance early this morning, so will 
hedge toward global guidance (which often does not suffer 
impacts of convective effects). Such a hedge favors the track of
the low passing directly from LaSalle to Chicago this evening 
while deepening a mb or two per hour. With this in mind, will 
have to watch for a narrow window for moisture-driven surface- 
based instability to sneak along and east of I-55 this evening 
(5 to 9 PM) to support low-topped convection along or just ahead
of the synoptic cold front. The overlap of strongly veering 
low-level wind profiles within the low-centroid and high
moisture-driven convective layer does raise concern for low-
topped supercell structures, though would have to think they 
would be harmless given limited opportunity for breaks in cloud 
cover to steepen low-level lapse rates (effectively limiting the
opportunity for truly surface-based convection). In the off 
chance that the surface low moves even further north than 
expected AND there is partial sunshine in the narrow warm sector
to steepen low-level lapse rates, cannot discount a threat for 
a brief tornado. At this point, we assess the chance of such an 
outcome to be very low (less than 5%), a sentiment that is 
shared by SPC (we did check in with them this morning). So, will
continue to withhold mentioning a threat for severe weather 
today in the HWO and graphical products and allow for 
observations this afternoon guide adjustments in strategy, if 
needed. 

In the immediate wake of the cold front this evening, initial 
pressure rises on the order of 2 to 3 mb/hr will drive a period 
of westerly winds gusting 30 to 35 mph. Robust cold air 
advection will send temperatures falling into the upper 40s to 
lower 50s overnight with wind chills by daybreak Friday solidly 
in the low to mid 40s. The overnight period is favored to be dry
for most areas, though can envision a few showers continuing 
near and southeast of I-57 near and just behind the cold front. 


Friday: 

On Friday, the northern-stream trough will whip through the 
Great Lakes anchored by a seasonably cool 500mb temperatures 
near -25C. A low-level trowel-like structure within the 
cyclonic shear axis of the trough will support a diurnal flare 
of showers with peak coverage during the afternoon hours across 
the area. Pressure rises will actually be greatest during the 
afternoon (+10mb/6hr) as a 1040mb surface high builds into the 
plains. As a result, the expectation is for a period of strong 
north to northwesterly winds Friday afternoon, peaking in the 35
to 40 mph range. Locally higher gusts of 45 to 55 mph cannot be
ruled out in the tallest showers. Extensive stratus and 
continued cold air advection will limit highs to the lower 50s, 
though would not be surprised if temperatures remain in the 
upper 40s as hinted by more aggressive deterministic guidance. 

As the upper-level trough whips overhead, tumbling temperatures
atop the warm waters of Lake Michigan will set the stage for 
the blossoming of lake effect rain showers. With inversion 
heights progged to climb to nearly 20kft and above the
minus 20C level, cannot rule out a few lightning strikes and 
graupel (soft hail) in the deepest lake effect convective cores.
